hints.quote: You'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones. There's the amine classification, that's gonna be your epinephrine, your norepinephrine. There's peptide hormones, like insulin, and steroid hormones, like estrogen or testosterone.
hints.take: Know the three classes with an example of each, and that steroids act on receptors inside the cell while peptides bind on the surface.

hints.quote: Because that lower jaw will grow in somebody who has acromegaly. The hands and the feet as well, but look for the jaw in your patients.
hints.take: Acromegaly in an adult shows the dentist a growing mandible: a bite moving from Class I to edge-to-edge or Class III, new diastemas and a large tongue.

hints.quote: I don't want to place an implant when their face and their body's still growing, because everything's going to move around that implant, but that implant's going to be stuck in that bone.
hints.take: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates; plan a young patient's implant for after growth stops.

hints.quote: The first thing they have to do when they're doing these surgeries is they have to identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Because if you damage that nerve, it actually affects the patient's vocal cords.
hints.take: Thyroid and parathyroid surgery puts the recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk: damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually for good.

hints.quote: Hypothyroidism is something you'll see far more frequently.
hints.take: Expect hypothyroid patients (fatigue, weight gain, macroglossia, slow healing, usually on thyroid hormone) far more often than hyperthyroid ones.

hints.quote: It is a life-threatening emergency. You'll see a high fever, you'll see a rapid heart rate, sometimes as much as 140 or higher. So if you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911.
hints.take: Thyroid storm: high fever, a pulse of 140 or more, agitation and delirium in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism; call 911.

hints.quote: So you need to understand the calcium metabolism side of this, and also its effects on oral and maxillofacial bone.
hints.take: Know what PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin each do, and read hyperparathyroidism on a radiograph: lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, loose teeth.

hints.quote: An increase in ACTH production stimulates melanocytes.
hints.take: He said he hadn't given the class this one, so he told them: in Addison disease low cortisol lets ACTH rise, and ACTH darkens the skin and oral mucosa.

hints.quote: Sometimes you have to give them supplemental corticosteroids after a bigger procedure. It would be best to talk with their doctor and find out how much you want to prescribe them before you do that.
hints.take: An Addison patient can't raise cortisol for surgical stress: know the crisis triggers (long surgery, infection or trauma, a missed dose) and plan extra steroid with the physician.

hints.quote: If you have a patient who has an HbA1c that's greater than 7, that means it's poorly controlled, and they're at much higher risk of failure of implants, they're higher risk of periodontal disease.
hints.take: Above 7 percent is poor control (more implant failure and periodontal disease); below 7 is well controlled, and a person without diabetes runs about 5.

hints.quote: I will warn you that some of these CGMs only read down to a certain level.
hints.take: If a patient looks hypoglycemic, check a finger-stick even when the CGM shows a number: his patient's read 53 while she was in the 30s.

hints.quote: Typically a straight glucose solution is a better option because it requires less processing through the liver and quicker increase in the blood sugar.
hints.take: Give straight glucose, not table sugar (half fructose); if oral glucose fails, IV dextrose or glucagon IM or subcutaneously, and expect a slow response on a GLP-1 drug.

hints.quote: One pack per day times how many years they've been doing it, that's how you get your pack year history. Don't forget that. You'll need to know that next year for clinic.
hints.take: Pack-years = packs per day times years smoked: one pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years.

hints.quote: Remember, type 2 diabetes patients are typically hyperinsulinemic, they're just not… it's not working like it's supposed to.
hints.take: In type 2 diabetes insulin is ineffective, not deficient; autoimmune beta-cell destruction is type 1.
His aside that alcohol lowers ADH and nicotine raises it was offered as trivia; know ADH's job and diabetes insipidus instead.

dental: Hormone classes: amine = epinephrine, peptide = insulin, steroid = estrogen. Steroids bind intracellular receptors.
Anterior pituitary: ACTH (adrenal cortex), TSH (thyroid), GH (growth), FSH and LH (reproduction), prolactin (lactation). Posterior: ADH (water; diabetes insipidus) and oxytocin.

GH persists for life; puberty's sex hormones fuse the growth plates (wait for growth to stop before an implant). Excess before puberty: very tall; after: acromegaly, a growing mandible (Class I to Class III), diastemas, macroglossia, prognathism.
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery: the recurrent laryngeal nerve is found first; damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually permanent.
Hyperthyroid: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance; increased epinephrine sensitivity, avoid excessive vasoconstrictor when uncontrolled; accelerated eruption in children.
Hypothyroid (seen far more often than hyper): fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia; delayed eruption, macroglossia, delayed wound healing.

Thyroid storm (thyroid crisis, thyrotoxic crisis): rare; large hormone release in a short time; high fever, heart rate 140 or higher, agitation, shakiness, nausea, delirium, hypertension. Life-threatening: call 911.
PTH = fast acting: osteoclasts (resorption), kidney calcium reabsorption, calcitriol so the gut absorbs calcium. Vitamin D = long-term, activated in the kidney.
Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
Hyperparathyroidism in the mouth: loss of lamina dura (the white line of socket bone the PDL attaches to), radiolucent brown tumors (refer to the physician), tooth mobility.
Hypoparathyroidism: hypocalcemia, neuromuscular irritability, tetany.
Cortex: cortisol (stress, immunity, glucose) and aldosterone (sodium retention, potassium). Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine (vasoconstrictors, stress management).
Addison: hypotension, fatigue, hyperpigmentation; diffuse oral melanosis because high ACTH stimulates melanocytes.

Adrenal crisis triggers: long or stressful surgery, significant infection or trauma, missed steroid medication; after a big procedure, extra corticosteroid, dose set with the physician. Signs: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness, shock.
Cushing: moon face, buffalo hump, hyperglycemia; increased infection risk and delayed healing.
Alpha cells: glucagon (glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis). Beta cells: insulin (glucose into cells, storage).

Type 1 = autoimmune beta-cell destruction (insulin to survive). Type 2 = insulin resistance with hyperinsulinemia: insulin ineffective, not deficient. HbA1c: about 5 normal, below 7 well controlled, above 7 poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease).
Diabetes in the mouth: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, more periodontal disease and caries. The perio link is bidirectional.
Poor diabetic healing: decreased neutrophil function, poor blood supply, impaired collagen synthesis.

Diabetic visit: review control and HbA1c, confirm meal and medication (metformin plus no breakfast: watch for a low), morning appointment. Hypoglycemia (sweating, tremors, confusion, tachycardia): finger-stick (a CGM may stop at its floor), under 60 give straight glucose, not table sugar; slow on a GLP-1 drug; IV dextrose or glucagon IM/subQ if it fails; unconscious, emergency protocols.
Puberty: gingival inflammation. Pregnancy: pregnancy gingivitis, pyogenic granuloma. Menopause: xerostomia, altered taste, osteoporosis.
Pack-years = packs per day times years smoked (1 pack a day for 40 years = 40).

sections.title: Before you treat
items: Hyperthyroid, especially uncontrolled: use epinephrine-containing anesthetics cautiously; avoid excessive vasoconstrictor.
Diabetic: review glycemic control and HbA1c; confirm the meal and medication; morning appointment; watch for hypoglycemia.
Addison disease: a long or stressful surgery, an infection or trauma, or a missed steroid dose can set off adrenal crisis.
Cushing syndrome: plan for infection risk and delayed healing.
Hyperparathyroidism: look for loss of lamina dura, brown tumors and mobility on the exam and radiographs.
Pregnant patient: pregnancy gingivitis and pyogenic granuloma.
